Title: Flowers for a Child's Grave: Gentle Choices and Keeping the Dates
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
The graves of children are the most tended graves in any cemetery. Parents visit for decades. Birthdays are kept, holidays are decorated, and the small section where infants are buried is often the most colorful part of the grounds. If you are a parent, this guide is for the practical side. If you are a friend or relative, it is for knowing what helps.

## What parents place
*   **Soft colors and small flowers.** Pastel pinks, blues, lavenders and whites; baby's breath, small roses, daisies, forget-me-nots. Arrangements for a child's grave are usually smaller and gentler than for an adult's.  
*   **The child's things.** A small toy, a pinwheel, a stuffed animal in a weatherproof bag, a balloon on a birthday. Many cemeteries relax their decoration rules for the children's section, and most crews leave a child's grave alone. Ask the office what is permitted; the answer is often more than the sign says.  
*   **Seasonal decorations.** Easter eggs, a small Christmas tree, Halloween pumpkins. Parents of young children decorate the grave the way they would have decorated the house.  
*   **Something for the birthday, every year.** The birthday is the date that matters most, and it is kept for as long as the parents live.

## What friends and family can send
For friends, the hard part is the years after. The first months bring cards and casseroles. The birthday two years on is spent alone. The single most valued thing a friend can do is remember the date: the birthday, and the anniversary. Flowers placed at the grave that day, with a note that uses the child's name, tell the parents that someone else is still counting.
Use the name. Parents of children who have died want to hear it and rarely do. "Thinking of Ellie today, and of you" is the whole message.

## For parents who live far away
Families move after a loss, for work or to start again, and the grave stays behind. That distance is felt on every birthday. A standing delivery for the birthday, the anniversary and the holidays, with a photo of the flowers at the small headstone, keeps the grave tended and keeps the parents part of it. Many parents describe the photo as the thing they had been afraid to ask anyone for.
BloomBridge places flowers at any grave in all 50 states on the dates you choose. A local Runner finds the grave, places the arrangement gently, and sends you a photo. The delivery photos build a memorial page for the child that family and friends can visit.

## Infant and pregnancy loss
Many cemeteries have a section for infants and stillborn babies, sometimes with a shared memorial for pregnancies lost too early for a grave. Flowers there are welcome and are usually left alone longer than elsewhere. Hospitals and support groups can tell you where the section is if the family does not know. October is Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month, and October 15 is the day many families mark it at the grave with a candle and flowers.

## A note on cemetery rules
The rules for a child's grave are usually enforced with a lighter hand, but they exist, and the annual clean-ups apply. Balloons and glass are the two things most often removed even from children's graves. Our guide to cemetery flower rules explains how to check with the office.

*   **Soft colors and small flowers.** Pastel pinks, blues, lavenders and whites; baby's breath, small roses, daisies, forget-me-nots. Arrangements for a child's grave are usually smaller and gentler than for an adult's.  
*   **The child's things.** A small toy, a pinwheel, a stuffed animal in a weatherproof bag, a balloon on a birthday. Many cemeteries relax their decoration rules for the children's section, and most crews leave a child's grave alone. Ask the office what is permitted; the answer is often more than the sign says.  
*   **Seasonal decorations.** Easter eggs, a small Christmas tree, Halloween pumpkins. Parents of young children decorate the grave the way they would have decorated the house.  
*   **Something for the birthday, every year.** The birthday is the date that matters most, and it is kept for as long as the parents live.
texts.2:
## What friends and family can send
For friends, the hard part is the years after. The first months bring cards and casseroles. The birthday two years on is spent alone. The single most valued thing a friend can do is remember the date: the birthday, and the anniversary. Flowers placed at the grave that day, with a note that uses the child's name, tell the parents that someone else is still counting.
Use the name. Parents of children who have died want to hear it and rarely do. "Thinking of Ellie today, and of you" is the whole message.
texts.3:
## For parents who live far away
Families move after a loss, for work or to start again, and the grave stays behind. That distance is felt on every birthday. A standing delivery for the birthday, the anniversary and the holidays, with a photo of the flowers at the small headstone, keeps the grave tended and keeps the parents part of it. Many parents describe the photo as the thing they had been afraid to ask anyone for.
BloomBridge places flowers at any grave in all 50 states on the dates you choose. A local Runner finds the grave, places the arrangement gently, and sends you a photo. The delivery photos build a memorial page for the child that family and friends can visit.
texts.4:
## Infant and pregnancy loss
Many cemeteries have a section for infants and stillborn babies, sometimes with a shared memorial for pregnancies lost too early for a grave. Flowers there are welcome and are usually left alone longer than elsewhere. Hospitals and support groups can tell you where the section is if the family does not know. October is Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month, and October 15 is the day many families mark it at the grave with a candle and flowers.
texts.5:
## A note on cemetery rules
The rules for a child's grave are usually enforced with a lighter hand, but they exist, and the annual clean-ups apply. Balloons and glass are the two things most often removed even from children's graves. Our guide to cemetery flower rules explains how to check with the office.

# The letter was to his mother, and it... - StarLife Documented | Facebook
## StarLife Documented's Post
The letter was to his mother, and it was about a daughter who had been gone for years. George Bush wrote letters his whole life, constantly, to everyone, but the ones to his mother, Dorothy, were their own steady thread, kept up across decades and distances no matter what else was happening. Dorothy Walker Bush had raised her children to compete hard and to never boast, and her son wrote to her the way you keep talking to the person who taught you how to be a person. Somewhere in that long correspondence is a letter that is not like the others. In 1953, George and his wife had lost their second child, a little girl named Robin, to leukemia. She was three. She had been sick for months, and they had carried her through it as far as love can carry anyone, and then she was gone, and the young couple did what that generation often did, which was to fold the grief inward and keep moving. But years later, a grown man with a full and demanding life sat down and wrote to his mother about missing his daughter. Not in the season of the loss. Long after. Long after the world would have assumed a busy man had made his peace and moved along. The letter exists because he needed to say it, and the person he needed to say it to was the one who had first shown him what a mother is. There is a particular thing that happens when a parent loses a small child. The child stays exactly that age forever, and the parent keeps getting older, and the distance between them grows by a year every year, and the ache does not close so much as travel alongside you. George Bush carried Robin like that. He spoke of her rarely and plainly when he did, and he kept her name in the family, and once, in a letter, he set the missing of her down on paper and sent it to his own mother, because some griefs you can only really say to the person who knew you before you were strong. He went on to a long life crowded with other people's attention. But in his own handwriting, kept and saved, there is a man telling his mother that he still missed a three-year-old. That was the part of him the public almost never got to read.

## StarLife Documented's Post
The letter was to his mother, and it was about a daughter who had been gone for years. George Bush wrote letters his whole life, constantly, to everyone, but the ones to his mother, Dorothy, were their own steady thread, kept up across decades and distances no matter what else was happening. Dorothy Walker Bush had raised her children to compete hard and to never boast, and her son wrote to her the way you keep talking to the person who taught you how to be a person. Somewhere in that long correspondence is a letter that is not like the others. In 1953, George and his wife had lost their second child, a little girl named Robin, to leukemia. She was three. She had been sick for months, and they had carried her through it as far as love can carry anyone, and then she was gone, and the young couple did what that generation often did, which was to fold the grief inward and keep moving. But years later, a grown man with a full and demanding life sat down and wrote to his mother about missing his daughter. Not in the season of the loss. Long after. Long after the world would have assumed a busy man had made his peace and moved along. The letter exists because he needed to say it, and the person he needed to say it to was the one who had first shown him what a mother is. There is a particular thing that happens when a parent loses a small child. The child stays exactly that age forever, and the parent keeps getting older, and the distance between them grows by a year every year, and the ache does not close so much as travel alongside you. George Bush carried Robin like that. He spoke of her rarely and plainly when he did, and he kept her name in the family, and once, in a letter, he set the missing of her down on paper and sent it to his own mother, because some griefs you can only really say to the person who knew you before you were strong. He went on to a long life crowded with other people's attention. But in his own handwriting, kept and saved, there is a man telling his mother that he still missed a three-year-old. That was the part of him the public almost never got to read.

Title: flowers on graves, 1850-1930
Chunks: 10,11,12,13,22,23,24,25,37,38,39,40
The employment of flowers, and the cultivation of funereal emblems, led to care of the sacred depository. This has existed throughout all nations. Plato regarded the care of the monuments of their predecessors, and the performance of the funereal rites to their friends, as payments justly due to the dead. The Chinese, and other nations esteemed barbarous, pay visits to the grave, and perform ceremonies to their deceased relatives long after the period of their death. In Ireland funeral ceremonies performed upon a particular day are common. The English are almost the only people who do not pay those reverential and affectionate visits, and who do not generally decorate the grave with flowers, &c. The Welsh practise this amiable duty very generally. It is referred to in the following Epitaph at Longhor churchyard, Glamorganshire:
The village maidens to her grave shall bring
Selected garlands each returning spring—
Selected sweets—in emblem of the maid
Who underneath this hallow’d turf is laid;
Like her they flourish, beauteous to the eye;
Like her, too soon, they languish, fade, and die.
Another Welsh epitaph formed on the custom of planting flowers on the grave speaks unfavourably as to the enjoyment of connubial bliss:
This spot is the sweetest I’ve seen in my life,
For it raises my flowers and covers my wife.
Many serious epitaphs from an early period might, however, be cited illustrative of the practice. At St. Margaret’s, Westminster, are the following lines to Elizabeth Hereicke :—
Sweet Virgin, that I do not set
Thy Grave-Verse up in mournful Jet
Or dappled Marble, let thy Shade
Not wrathfull seeme, or fright the Maid,
Who hither at her weeping Howers
Shall come to strew thy Earth with Flowers:
No: know blest Soule, where there’s not one
Remainder left of Brasse, or Stone:
Thy living Epitaph shall be
Though lost in them yet found in me:
Deare in thy Bed of Roses then,
Till this World shall dissolve (as Men)
Sleepe : while we hide thee from the Light,
Drawing thy Curtains round—_Good Night._
I close this essay in the words of Mrs. Hemans, inscribed as an Epitaph at Bathampton.

Bring flowers, pale flowers, o’er the grave to shed,
A crown for the brow of the early dead;
Though they smile in vain for what once was ours,
They are Love’s last gift—bring flowers, pale flowers.
**Pettigrew, Thomas Joseph, Chronicles of the Tombs: A Select Collection of Epitaphs, … (London: 1857), (in a chapter entitled ‘Funeral Emblems’ pp. 261-272**
**1858**
p. 114
I made a visit to one of the most favourite and fashionable of English cemeteries. {many stonemason’s yards in the vicinity} a more beautiful and luxurious garden it is impossible to conceive. The season was autumn, and every path was radiant with dahlias, fuchsias, verbenas, heliotrope, salvias, lobelias, geraniums, monthly roses and ~ other flowers. [I thought] African and French marigolds there in bad taste. In some country churchyards, where the custom of planting flowers is most rife, none are thought of that are not sweet scented. Merely beautiful looking flowers are never admitted, though it is said that these are sometimes planted by stealth, as a sort of satire, on the grave of an unpopular person.
But on the graves of beloved ones the homely sweet scented rosemary, the aconite, the snow-drop, the violet, the lily of the valley; and the rose are suitable to churchyard or cemetery. {The mignioette, laurustinus (winter flowering), arbutus also suitable} and form a beautiful relief to the gloomy cypress and dismal yew, which are often planted so closely together at the head and foot of the grave that they hardly have room to grow.}
p. 116
I came to a placard noting that: ‘The company undertake to turf and plant graves, and to maintain and keep them in order on the following terms. [prices left blank]’
p. 275 … and in Wales, to this day, not only are roses planted round graves, but it is usual to keep the graves freshly strewn over, for twelve months, with green herbs and flowers.

There is a grave in Wimbledon churchyard, of recent erection, which is quite a cultivated little garden. A few words engraven on the reverse of the headstone, pray the passer by not to pluck the flowers.
**Stone, Elizabeth, God’s Acre: or historical notices relating to churchyards, (1858), p. 275**
**1858**
**Full account of the funeral of**REV. DAVID D. EVANS, Baptist minister,
The _funeral_ took place at Pontrhydyrun Chapel, on Tuesday. The corpse lay at the residence of Mr. C. Conway, at Pontnewydd, and was borne on foot, in procession, to the chapel, along the turnpike road, amidst a very large assemblage of persons. As the procession left Mr Conway’s grounds, the crowd assembled uncovered in token of respect, and then followed the arranged procession. The Rev. E. Hands, minister of the place, and the Rev. S. Price, of Abersychan, officiated on the occasion. As the coffin was lowered into the vault, several very handsome bouquets of _flowers_ were cast upon it, a tribute of pleasing recollection contributed, we understand, by Mrs Charles Cairns, of Newport.
**Monmouthshire Merlin, 11th September 1858**
**1858 North Wales**
‘A Mythology of Death’
‘Of all the fine memories of my stay in Wales I found nothing more moving than to visit the churchyards of the surrounding villages. Here I would often sit on the flat graves, among the flowers and bushes, … And then, in the scent of the grave-flowers, I could believe I was inhaling some other but related life.

{at a funeral} ‘Each of the followers {to the coffin} carries two sprigs of rosemary, one of which he casts into the grave. … The friends of the departed bestrew his grave with flowers, border it with slates, [the editor suggests this came in part from Peter Roberts, Cambrian Popular Antiquities, p. 177] and cover it with a stone slab on which are inscribed some words in memory of the deceased. The tombstones and crosses of our German village churchyards are not found in Wales. But instead they are all the more richly provided with the lively decoration of the flowers; they could be called gardens of death. Evergreens and bunches of flowers adorn every grave; the gravestones are washed at Easter, Whitsun and Christmas, and on Palm Sunday and at Easter pansies, wild roses, daffodils and rosemary are planted. This sad but friendly business is called “dressing the dead”, for at the time that every living person thinks it his duty to wear something new, so the dead too should not lack a new token of love.
**Rodenberg, Julius, (1831-), Ein Herbst in Wales, Land and Leute, Marchen under Lieder, (****Hanover, 1858)****,****Translated by William Linnard, ‘An Autumn in Wales, (1856), Country and People, Tales and Songs’, (Cowbridge, 1985)****, chapter on ‘A Mythology of Death**’**,****pp. 93-94**
In many parts, and especially in South Wales, the friends of the deceased take much and laudable pains to deck the graves with flowers. A bordering of slates or stones, is nicely run around it, and the top bound in by stones, laid with taste, in a tessellated manner, which has an ornamental effect, whilst it remains a monument of a pious affection, gratified in paying its last tribute to a beloved or revered object.
**Roberts, Peter, The Cambrian Popular Antiquities of Wales, (1815), pp. 177-178**
**1858 (and earlier?) Briton Ferry**
The churchyard is much admired, the custom of planting evergreens and flowers over the graves of departed friends being here observed with peculiar care.

The Practice to which ‘Dol’ refers, of the annual frequenting of churchyards and the decking of graves on a prescribed day is a practice more common in south than north Wales, and especially so, still, in Monmouthshire by all ranks, social positions and religious belief. Flowering Sunday is Palm Sunday. They sprinkle the grave with flowers, or put them in a vessel with water, or plant them (including Snow of the Mountains found in the higher gradients of Monmouthshire). This is found in every graveyard throughout the ancient part of Gwent. Some might think that this is a horticultural competition. The correspondent says that he has never met with such a practice in north Wales.
**From Bye-Gones, vol 1, (January 1872) p. 23 (responding to Dol, Nov, 1871, p. 12)**
**1871, Llansantffraid-ym-Mechain, Montgomeryshire**
Easter Sunday
The churchyard looks very pretty on this day. The graves are all beautifully decked with flowers of various colours, and with evergreens, lavender, box and laurel being the favourites; and no pains are considered too great to be taken by friends and relatives for the adornment of the graves of their departed kinsmen and friends. I remember seeing a gentleman who had forgotten to send flowers the day before, turning to gather some which grew in the churchyard, for the purpose of decking his little daughter’s grave. The only reason given by the common people for this custom is that they wish to show a mark of respect for their departed friends, and that they have not forgotten them.
**Jones, Thomas Griffiths, (Cyffin)_, ‘A history of the Parish of Llansantffraid-ym-Mechain’, Montgomery Collections,_ vol. IV., (1871), p. 136**
**1872**
A custom also existed, but not peculiar to Wales, of the mourners carrying sprigs of Rosemary which they threw into the grave as soon as the service was finished. This was done at a burial at Gresford about 20 years ago, and the custom probably still exists. p. 332

The sowing of hemp seed on all hallows eve is not peculiar to Wales. The seed is sown a little before midnight. The sower is supposed to see a future partner or a coffin. p. 334
**Barnwell, E.L., Some Ancient Welsh Customs and Furniture, _Archaeologia Cambrensis_, 1872**
**1873**
TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT
At the adjourned inquest on Thursday only evidence of identification was taken. There was then an adjournment for a fortnight, by which time it is thought Captain Tyler will have completed his official investigation on behalf of the Board of Trade.
FUNERAL OF FOUR OF THE VICTIMS
The funeral of Thomas Wark, aged 10 years, Maggie Wark, 8 years, Ruby Wark, and Alice Minnett, nurse to the above, who were killed in the recent railway accident at Wigan, took place on Wednesday, at the Highgate Cemetery, London. The funeral cortege left the residence of Mr Andrew Wark, Old Hall, Highgate, at half-past twelve by the rear of the house, which abuts on to the cemetery. The four coffins, which were borne on men’s shoulders, ware covered with black cloth, without ornaments of any kind. Over each of the coffins were thrown a black velvet pail, edged with white, on which rested **wreaths of white flowers**. … All the deceased were interred in one grave, flowers being thrown in by some of the friends of the family.
**County Observer and Monmouthshire Central Advertiser, 16.8.1873**
**24.3.1874**
**Lady Day eve**
I went into [Clyro] churchyard and stood by Lily Crichton’s grave [died, aged 7, late 1873 or early 1874] … A wreath of flowers hung over the cross and some more flower wreaths lay upon the turf within the little enclosure framed by the marble coping and low iron railings. In the summer time a tall lily grows at the foot of the grave. … Mrs. Richard Williams was in the churchyard. She had come down from Paradise to trim Mr. Henry Venables’ grave.

**Francis Kilvert, Plomer, William, (ed), _Kilvert’s Diary_, 1977 edition, 3 vols, vol 2, p. 428**
**1875**
St. Pierre, in his beautiful “Harmonies of Nature,” after having dwelt with some earnestness on the propriety of planting flowers on graves, quotes this inscription, found engraven on an ancient tomb: “Au dehors je suis entoure de mauve et d’asphodele set au-dedans Je ne suis qu’un cadaver.” [Outside I am surrounded by mauve and asphodele set inside I am only a cadaver.]
**Cambrian, 10.9.1875**
**23.4.1875**
Funeral of Alice Grimshaw
A cross and a wreath of primroses and daisies made by Mary Cole’s nice children rested, one at the head, the other at the foot of the open grave. Mary Cole said her girls were very ‘good children for flowering anyone’
**Francis Kilvert, Plomer, William, (ed), _Kilvert’s Diary_, vol. 3 (1977), p. 176-177**
**1876**
THE EVICTION OF NONCONFORMISTS FROM THEIR CHAPEL IN CARDIGANSHIRE. DANGERS TO NONCONFORMITY
On Sunday evening last a sermon on the above subject was delivered at the English Unitarian Chapel, Highland-place, by the Rev. J. Joseph George.

… Look at the old churchyard below! Why is it held in such affectionate remembrance? There lies the ashes of past generations who inhabited this valley, and whose names and memories are still held dear. Call to mind that memorable day, “flowering Sunday,” once so honoured and still honoured in many districts. Step into that country burying ground, watch those trembling hands strewing flowers upon that grave which are watered with tears of affectionate remembrance. Is there nothing in that? Is it all sentiment? Sentiment be religious, yea, divine. When the woman poured a box of ointment upon the head of Jesus his disciples were indignant, but he said “She hath wrought a good work upon me, wherever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her.” Sentiment if shown in love towards dead or living be good. Shall a tyrant’s word be enough to prevent a living love being poured out towards the dead? Surely, never.
**Aberdare Times, 25.11.1876**
**1877 Maelor Saesneg**
Sprigs of rosemary are thrown into the grave at the same time the sacristan sprinkles earth upon the body.
**Lee, M.H., Maelor Saesneg, (local traditions of), _Archaeologia Cambrensis_, (1877), p. 289**
**1880s Oxfordshire**
Had the custom of sending wreaths to funerals been general then [1880s] as it is today [1930s] they [the villagers] would certainly have subscribed their last halfpenny for the purpose. But, at that time, the coffins of the country poor went flowerless to the grave …
**Thompson, Flora,_Lark Rise,_ (1939), ‘To Church on Sunday’**
**1882 location unspecified**

Now this beautiful custom, common enough as it has again become in our time, had fallen completely out of use in England a hundred or more years ago (perhaps it died a natural death when the heavy Hanovarian Georges came to our land), and then appeared singularly beautiful in the eyes of the tourists who visited Wales and had only been accustomed to the heavy woe that marked an English funeral, where pomp and ostentation vied with grief in paying the last sad rites to the departed when hired mercenaries stood around the rich man’s door in cumbrous black, and adorned with weeds and weepers, with faces prostituted to grief, while carousers within doors devoured the huge funereal meats, and often got heavy, or light, on strong beer, or yet stronger spirits. Such a show-an insult to real heartfelt grief and now happily curtailed (though too much of it lingers yet) is in marked contrast to the simple village ceremonies of Wales, where although a solemn festival a large scale prevails, and mourners or followers flock in numbers incredible, is void of that formal parade that marked old English interments. What more beautiful than “when a young unmarried person dies, his or her ways to the grave are strewed with sweet flowers and evergreens? and on such occasions it was the usual phrase that those persons are going to their nuptial beds, and not to their graves.
The custom of planting flowers, and placing cut flowers on graves, is a very pleasing one, and it is all friends can do outwardly thus to affectionately tend the resting places of their beloved ones who have gone on before them to that country “from whence no traveller returns”.
At Briton Ferry for generations, and perhaps ages, the planting of evergreens over the graves of departed friends, and bedecking them with flowers at certain seasons, particularly on Palm Sunday, has been observed.
These to review with more than annual care,
That wakeful love with pensive step will go.
**Malkin** says, “In the Easter week most generally the graves are newly dressed and manured with fresh earth, when such flowers or evergreens be wanted or wished for are planted. In the Whitsuntide holidays, or rather the preceding week, the graves are again looked after, weeded and otherwise dressed, or, if necessary planted again. This work the nearest relatives of the deceased always do with their own hands and never by servants or hired persons.

“Yet fancy, empress of the realms of song,
Shall bless the decent mode, and reason own
It might be right – for who can prove it wrong?
The same writer says: My father-in-law’s grave, in Cowbridge church, has been strewed by his surviving servants every Sunday morning for these twenty years.”
The practice in some places of putting flowers or evergreens within the coffin has been objected to by some writers on the ground that the decay must hasten decomposition.
The Almighty fiat [sic] has gone forth that man return to the dust from whence he sprang we may try to copy the old Egyptians in their mode of embalming; we may ossify the corpse, or turn it into leather in the pattern of Jeremy Bentham, yet do what we may, or all we can, to dust sooner or later we shall all return. The ancient Egyptians had reason is what they did in the fine art of embalming, which is happily lost, for according to their belief the soul could not pass into Hades so long as the body remained intact, but with us who hold a purer faith, why delay the course of nature ? The grave of the old ballad is after all a reasonable one:
Lay me a green sod under my head,
And another at my feet;
And lay my bent bow by my side,
Which was my music sweet;
And make my grave of gravel and green,
Which is most right and meet.
Let me have length and breadth enough,
With a green sod under my head:
That they may say, when I am dead,
Here lies bold Robin Hood.
“O while they Season of flowers, and thy tender spray, thick of leaves, remain, I will pluck the roses from the brakes; the flowerets of the meads, and gems of the woods; the vivid trefoils, beauties of the ground, and the gaily smiling bloom of the verdant herbs, humbly will I lay them on the grave of Ivor!” So said old Dafydd ap Gwilym, the bard
I hope the reader will not find this lugubrious notice tiresome, as I purpose writing more on Welsh funeral customs some day.
**Cardiff Times, 23.4.1887**
**1887**

Flowers on the grave – how the custom has become part of all our funeral ceremonies! It seems sort of pitiful, forlorn-like now to see a flowerless coffin pass by in its car. At the funeral of the four victims to the incendiarism which burnt out Whiteley in Queen’s road, three of the coffins were profusely covered with lovely flowers the fourth was bare. When the tragic procession stopped at the open graves, before the officiating clergyman, a little flower girl ran forward and threw her stock in trade on the bare cover.
**Cardiff Times, 22.10.1887**
**1888**
FLOWERS ON GRAVES
The decision of Justices Wills and Grantham in the case of McGough v. the Lancaster Burial Board will cause some surprise. The plaintiff had purchased from the defendant Board the exclusive right of burial in a plot of ground in their cemetery, and had buried a child in it. He had not, however, obtained any right of erecting monuments. He placed on the grave a glass case containing flowers, and this the defendants, in the exercise of their general power of managing the cemetery, removed. The plaintiff brought an action for trespass in respect of this removal, and obtained judgment in his favour in the Lancaster County Court, but the judges of the High Court have now reversed it, and decided in favour of the defendants. The functions and powers of Burial Boards and of local authorities where they provide cemeteries are defined by several Acts of Parliament. By the Act of 1852 (which was extended beyond the metropolis in 1853). … similar powers are conferred on local authorities by the clauses of the Cemeteries Clauses Act, 1847 …

The custom of putting flowers on graves is very general, and, one would think, rather to be encouraged than prohibited. Few would be disposed to approve of the policy of a Board which forbids such a practice-the judges did not; but they had to decide an abstract question of legal right, and they held that the board were not trespassers when, in pursuance of their regulations, they had the flowers removed. The principle on which they went was that the plaintiff had purchased a right of burial and nothing more, and consequently could not complain of the removal of the flowers, which in strictness he had no right to place on the grave. The abstract question involved in the case is of genera importance, though the damages awarded were but small; and we are glad to see that leave to appeal has been given. There have been previous judgments where the circumstances have been somewhat similar, though not identical, in which judgment has been given in favour of the owners of graves which have been interfered with. An authoritative decision of the Court of Appeal settling the rights in such cases will be useful-_Sanitary Record_.
**Cardigan Observer, and General Advertiser For the Counties of Cardigan, Carmarthen and Pembroke, 7.1.1888**
**1890 Yale (near Wrexham)**
A Welsh Funeral Custom
The nurse who attended the deceased in the last hours to walk close after the horse or bier, carrying in a handkerchief slips of laurel, box, rosemary, yew and other evergreens to dress the grave. In some places the nearest female relation of the deceased paid some poor person for decorating the grave on the day of the funeral, Palm Sunday, Easter and Whitsuntide. This is called Diodlys and was given on a plate at the door of the house when the coffin was on the bier. It was usual in some parts of north Wales for the mourners to kneel on the grave, and there repeat the Lord’s Prayer, and dress the grave with flowers for several Sundays after the internment.
Quotes Dafydd ap Gwilym’s ‘From dewy lawns …

[Quoted from Bingley]

Inscription on a stone in Loughor churchyard, Glamorgan:

## Mother's Day activities for kids in school
### Mothers Day gifts from kids at school
Mother's Day gifts from kids at school should be made in class from the same materials so no child brings something bought: a handprint card, a paper flower, a photo frame, a bookmark or a questionnaire. Teachers can collect a small craft fee from the class fund, and every child takes home the same kind of gift in their own style.
Making Mother's Day gifts from kids at school in class also solves the fairness problem: no child arrives with an expensive bought present while another has nothing. A shared set of chart paper, glue and sketch pens is enough for 40 children.

## Mother's Day activities for kids in school
### An inclusion note for teachers
Not every child in the class lives with a mother. Some are raised by a grandmother, a father, an aunt, a guardian or two fathers; some have lost a mother; some mothers work far away. Mother's Day activities for kids in school work for everyone when they are worded as "for someone who looks after you" and the child decides who that is. The questionnaire can say "All about my special person"; the card can go to Nani. Tell parents in the note home that this option exists, and check with the class teacher about children whose mother has died before the week begins. It is a small change, and the child it matters to will remember it.

## What to wear for Mother's Day: twin with mom for the photo
For Mother's Day, dress children in something comfortable in a colour that matches Mummy's outfit, so the family photo looks coordinated without buying matching sets: a cotton dress or co-ord for a daughter, a collared shirt for a son, and the same colour family for everyone. Twinning demand peaks in Mother's Day week in India.
The family photo is the one Mother's Day activity every family does, and it is the one that gets printed. Two things make it work: the light (take it by a window before 10 a.m. or after 4 p.m.) and a shared colour. You do not need a matching mother–daughter set to twin: start with the child's outfit and pull the colour into the mother's saree, kurta or dress. INCLUD's guide to mother–daughter twinning outfits has the "daughter-first" method and colour combinations for Mother's Day and other occasions.
For daughters, the dresses for girls range (₹489 to ₹2,489) covers everyday cotton dresses and party styles; for a Sunday lunch out, the girls' party wear dresses are dressier. The Mother's Day edit (250 styles, ₹359 to ₹3,199 on 24 September 2026) brings together sets, casual dresses and party dresses in one place, and for the youngest, the 0–2 years baby girls' range has the first-Mother's-Day outfit. Sons can match in a boys' shirt in the same colour family.
A small matching touch works as well as a full outfit: a beaded bracelet set split between mother and daughter, or the same hair clips worn by both.

## What to wear for Mother's Day: twin with mom for the photo
### Mother's Day ideas: making the day about her, not the photo
Keep Mother's Day focused on her: the outfits, the photo and the gifts are there to make her feel seen, not to create more work. If dressing up or the photo stresses her, drop it. The best Mother's Day ideas are the ones she does not have to plan, cook, clean up after or arrange.
That is the last and most important of all the Mother's Day ideas on this page. The day often turns into another event she organises: she lays out the children's clothes, cooks the lunch, and takes the photo she is not in. Hand the camera to someone else. Put her in the picture.

## Frequently asked questions
When is Mother's Day in India in 2027?
Mother's Day in India in 2027 is on Sunday 9 May 2027. India follows the second-Sunday-of-May date used in the United States, so Mother's Day always falls between 8 and 14 May: it was 10 May in 2026 and will be 14 May in 2028. It is not a public holiday, so most schools celebrate on Friday 7 May or Saturday 8 May 2027.
Is Mother's Day a holiday in India?
No. Mother's Day in India is not a gazetted public holiday or a restricted holiday. It falls on a Sunday, so most offices and schools are closed anyway, and schools usually hold their Mother's Day activities for kids on the last working day before. It is a secular, family occasion rather than a religious festival.
What is the history of Mother's Day?
The modern Mother's Day began in the United States when Anna Jarvis held a memorial service for her mother in Grafton, West Virginia, on 10 May 1908, sending 500 white carnations. President Woodrow Wilson made the second Sunday of May a national observance in 1914. India adopted the American date; the UK's Mothering Sunday is a separate, older tradition in March.
Why are carnations given on Mother's Day?
Carnations became the Mother's Day flower because Anna Jarvis sent 500 white carnations, her mother's favourite flower, to the first service in 1908. The tradition grew of wearing a red or pink carnation for a living mother and a white one for a mother who had died. Children can make paper carnations or build one from a flower-block kit.
What are free Mother's Day activities for kids?
Free Mother's Day activities for kids include breakfast in bed made with what is at home, a handmade card, a coupon book of chores and hugs, a song or dance, a rangoli at the door, a terrace picnic, a walk to collect flowers, a recreated old photo, an interview about her childhood and a video call to the grandmothers. None needs a shop.
What can a 2 year old make for Mother's Day?

## Frequently asked questions
A 2-year-old can make a handprint flower bouquet, a fingerprint heart card, a sticker picture, or a sponge-painted card with an adult's help. Title: 5.8K views · 98 reactions | Every grave holds a story. Sometimes, all it takes is a flower to remind us that someone is still remembered. 🌼

For this part of my October cemetery series, I’m sharing the grave of Mollie Herlihy Parlin at South Lead Cemetery in Lead, South Dakota.

I visited her grave on her birthday, April 7th, at the request of a follower. He told me he had been bringing her a daisy every day, and since he couldn’t be there for her birthday, he asked if I would stop by. That simple act of kindness stayed with me.

Online burial records list her as Mollie, born April 7, 1870, in Michigan. She passed away on April 10, 1892 ~ just three days after her 22nd birthday. FamilySearch also identifies her as the mother of a little boy, Franklin Kendrick Parlin, born less than two months before her death.

As I looked around her grave, I didn’t notice any nearby headstones that appeared to belong to relatives. I don’t know her whole story, but there’s something about standing beside someone’s grave and taking a moment to wonder about the life behind the name.

If you’re ever looking for a small, meaningful thing to do, stop by the grave of someone you don’t know. Bring flowers, pick up litter around their resting place, or simply spend a quiet moment thinking about their life.

You don’t have to have known someone to remember them. 🙏

Stay tuned for more of my cemetery series throughout the month of October.

Elvia Bautista, 22, lives in Santa Rosa, Calif., where she works as a caregiver for the elderly and mentally handicapped. A high school dropout, Bautista now speaks to young people about the dangers of gang life. **Tatiana Harrison******hide caption****
**toggle caption**i
Tatiana Harrison
I believe that everyone deserves flowers on their grave.
When I go to the cemetery to visit my brother, it makes me sad to see graves -- just the cold stones -- and no flowers on them.
They look lonely, like nobody loves them. I believe this is the worst thing in the world -- that loneliness. No one to visit you and brush off the dust from your name and cover you with color. A grave without any flowers looks like the person has been forgotten. And then what was the point of even living -- to be forgotten?
Almost every day my brother's grave has something new on it: Flowers from me, or candles from the Dollar Store or an image of the Virgin Maria or shot glasses. There's even some little Homies, these little toys that look like gangsters.
Sponsor Message
Once my brother's homies even put a bunch of marijuana on there for him -- I think my mother took it away. I think she also took away the blue rag someone put there for him one day.
Sometimes, when I bring flowers, I fix the flowers on the graves around my brother's grave. Some of the headstones have birthdates near my brother's; they are young, too. But many of them, if they have any little toys or things on them, those are red.

# Remembering All the Boys
#### Remembering All the Boys
All around my brother are boys who grew up to like red, making them the enemies of my brother. My brother was 16 when he was shot by someone who liked red, who killed him because he liked blue. And when I go to the cemetery I put flowers on the graves of the boys who liked red, too.
Sometimes I go to the cemetery with one of my best friends, who had a crush on a boy who liked red, who was killed at 18 by someone who liked blue. And we will go together and bring a big bunch of flowers, enough for both of these boys whose families are actually even from the same state in Mexico.
Sponsor Message
There is no one but me and a few of my friends who go to both graves. Some people think it's a bad idea. Some people think it's heroic.
I think they're both being silly. I don't go to try and disrespect some special rules or stop any kind of war. I go because I believe that no matter where you came from or what you believed in, when you die, you want flowers on your grave and people who visit you and remember you that way.
I'm not any kind of traitor or any kind of hero. I am the sister of Rogelio Bautista, and I say his name so you will hear it and be one more person that remembers him. I want everyone to remember all the boys, red and blue, in my cemetery. When we remember, we put flowers on their graves.

Elvia Bautista, 22, lives in Santa Rosa, Calif., where she works as a caregiver for the elderly and mentally handicapped. A high school dropout, Bautista now speaks to young people about the dangers of gang life. **Tatiana Harrison******hide caption****
**toggle caption**i
Tatiana Harrison
I believe that everyone deserves flowers on their grave.
When I go to the cemetery to visit my brother, it makes me sad to see graves -- just the cold stones -- and no flowers on them.
They look lonely, like nobody loves them. I believe this is the worst thing in the world -- that loneliness. No one to visit you and brush off the dust from your name and cover you with color. A grave without any flowers looks like the person has been forgotten. And then what was the point of even living -- to be forgotten?
Almost every day my brother's grave has something new on it: Flowers from me, or candles from the Dollar Store or an image of the Virgin Maria or shot glasses. There's even some little Homies, these little toys that look like gangsters.
Sponsor Message
Once my brother's homies even put a bunch of marijuana on there for him -- I think my mother took it away. I think she also took away the blue rag someone put there for him one day.
Sometimes, when I bring flowers, I fix the flowers on the graves around my brother's grave. Some of the headstones have birthdates near my brother's; they are young, too. But many of them, if they have any little toys or things on them, those are red.

# Remembering All the Boys
#### Remembering All the Boys
All around my brother are boys who grew up to like red, making them the enemies of my brother. My brother was 16 when he was shot by someone who liked red, who killed him because he liked blue. And when I go to the cemetery I put flowers on the graves of the boys who liked red, too.
Sometimes I go to the cemetery with one of my best friends, who had a crush on a boy who liked red, who was killed at 18 by someone who liked blue. And we will go together and bring a big bunch of flowers, enough for both of these boys whose families are actually even from the same state in Mexico.
Sponsor Message
There is no one but me and a few of my friends who go to both graves. Some people think it's a bad idea. Some people think it's heroic.
I think they're both being silly. I don't go to try and disrespect some special rules or stop any kind of war. I go because I believe that no matter where you came from or what you believed in, when you die, you want flowers on your grave and people who visit you and remember you that way.
I'm not any kind of traitor or any kind of hero. I am the sister of Rogelio Bautista, and I say his name so you will hear it and be one more person that remembers him. I want everyone to remember all the boys, red and blue, in my cemetery. When we remember, we put flowers on their graves.

Title: 5.8K views · 98 reactions | Every grave holds a story. Sometimes, all it takes is a flower to remind us that someone is still remembered. 🌼

For this part of my October cemetery series, I’m sharing the grave of Mollie Herlihy Parlin at South Lead Cemetery in Lead, South Dakota.

I visited her grave on her birthday, April 7th, at the request of a follower. He told me he had been bringing her a daisy every day, and since he couldn’t be there for her birthday, he asked if I would stop by. That simple act of kindness stayed with me.

Online burial records list her as Mollie, born April 7, 1870, in Michigan. She passed away on April 10, 1892 ~ just three days after her 22nd birthday. FamilySearch also identifies her as the mother of a little boy, Franklin Kendrick Parlin, born less than two months before her death.

As I looked around her grave, I didn’t notice any nearby headstones that appeared to belong to relatives. I don’t know her whole story, but there’s something about standing beside someone’s grave and taking a moment to wonder about the life behind the name.

If you’re ever looking for a small, meaningful thing to do, stop by the grave of someone you don’t know. Bring flowers, pick up litter around their resting place, or simply spend a quiet moment thinking about their life.

You don’t have to have known someone to remember them. 🙏

Stay tuned for more of my cemetery series throughout the month of October.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
​
But maybe if more people thought about them before another family had to, fewer parents would have to face that burden alone.
​There are cemetery plots sitting unused all over this country.
Most people do not think about them that way.
They think about them only when they are handling an estate, sorting through papers, cleaning out a parent’s house, or trying to figure out what to do with something that was purchased years ago by someone they loved. A deed. A burial right. A cemetery space. A plot in a place nobody in the family lives near anymore.
It might sit in a file cabinet.
It might be listed in estate paperwork.
It might come up after a mother or father passes away and the children are trying to divide responsibilities, close accounts, sell the house, finish the paperwork, and make decisions nobody really wants to make.
And buried inside all of that is a cemetery plot.
Maybe two.
Maybe more.
A space purchased decades ago that no longer fits the family plan. Maybe the person who bought it was buried somewhere else. Maybe the family moved. Maybe siblings now live in different states. Maybe cremation changed the original plan. Maybe nobody knows what to do with it, so it just sits there.
To that family, it may feel like one more loose end.
To another family, it could become sacred ground.
That is the part most people never see.
While thousands of cemetery plots sit unused, families who lose a child are often blindsided by the cost, confusion, and emotional weight of needing one.
Nobody prepares for that.
Young families are not thinking about cemetery plots. They are thinking about pregnancy, names, bottles, cribs, car seats, hospital bags, baby clothes, ultrasounds, birthdays, and the life they are trying to build.
They are not thinking about burial space.
They are not thinking about opening and closing fees.
They are not thinking about cemetery rules.
They are not thinking about where they would go if the unthinkable happened.
Then loss comes.
Planning after a loss
Sometimes during pregnancy. Sometimes at birth. Sometimes after days or weeks in the NICU. Sometimes suddenly, after a baby came home. Sometimes in a way no family ever saw coming.
And before the family can even understand what happened, the questions begin.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
*   Where will the baby be buried?

*   Is there a cemetery nearby?

*   Is there a section for infants?

*   How much does a burial plot cost?

*   What fees are separate?

*   \Can we afford this?

*   Who do we call?

*   What happens now?
Burial Plot FAQ
That is a terrible moment to learn how expensive and confusing burial can be.
And this is where people need to understand something deeper.
For a grieving family, this is not just “a funeral.”
A funeral is an event.
A burial place is different.
A funeral happens on a day. A permanent place to return to lasts for years. It becomes the place a parent visits when nobody knows what to say. The place where flowers are brought. The place where a sibling may bring a drawing. The place where a family can sit in silence because love still needs somewhere to go.
That place matters.
After infant loss, remembrance is not a small thing.
It is not extra.
It is not just sentimental.
It is one of the ways a family keeps their baby from disappearing into silence.
Because when a baby dies, the world often moves on quickly. People may stop saying the name. They may avoid bringing it up because they are afraid of causing pain. They may think silence is kindness.
But for the family, silence can feel like erasure.
A resting place helps push back against that.
It says, “This child was here.”
It says, “This life mattered.”
It says, “There is a place in this world connected to this name.”
That matters when the life was brief. It matters when there are not years of photos, stories, school pictures, birthday parties, and memories for the world to hold onto. It matters when the love was enormous, but the visible proof of that life feels painfully small.
A cemetery plot is not just land.
It is not just grass.
It is not just a square on a map.
For a baby, it can become the only public place in the world where their name stands permanently.
That is why unused cemetery plots matter so much.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
There are families right now holding onto burial spaces they may never use. Not because they are selfish. Not because they do not care. Most of the time, they probably have not even thought about what that space could mean to someone else.
It is just part of the estate.
Part of the paperwork.
Part of the past.
Something to deal with eventually.
But imagine looking at it differently.
Imagine that the plot your family no longer needs could become the place another family visits for the rest of their lives.
Imagine that instead of sitting unused, it becomes the place where a baby’s name remains in the world.
Imagine that a space connected to one family’s history could become mercy for another family’s heartbreak.
That is what cemetery plot donation can do.
It turns something forgotten into something holy.
It turns a loose end into a lasting gift.
It turns unused space into a place for love and memory.
And for the person donating, there may also be a practical benefit. A cemetery plot donation to a qualified nonprofit may be treated as a noncash charitable contribution, and donors should speak with their tax advisor about whether they may qualify for a tax deduction, what documentation is needed, and how the plot should be valued. The IRS says Form 8283 is generally used when claiming more than $500 in noncash charitable contributions, and deductions over $5,000 for noncash items generally require additional documentation such as Section B of Form 8283 and a qualified appraisal.
That matters.
Because sometimes people want to help but do not know how. Sometimes they are settling an estate and trying to make responsible decisions. Sometimes they are asking, “Can we sell this? Transfer it? Donate it? Is it worth anything? Does anyone need it?”
Yes.
Someone may need it more than you can imagine.
And while the tax benefit may help make the decision easier, the deeper value is not found on a form.
The deeper value is this:

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
*   A family who lost a baby may not have to fight for a place.

*   A child may have somewhere their name can remain.

*   Love may have somewhere to return.

*   I think about the families who visit years later.

*   Not only in the first week.

*   Not only on the day of burial.

*   Years later.
A parent standing there on a birthday that most people forgot. A family stopping by on a holiday. Someone bringing flowers on a day that still hurts. A sibling growing up and slowly understanding that there was another child in the family, a baby whose life was brief but whose place is still real.
People may not see those moments.
They happen quietly.
No big announcement.
No attention.
Just love returning to the same place again and again.
That is what a donated plot can make possible.
It gives a family more than help with child funeral costs. It gives them a place that continues after the funeral is over.
Because after the service ends, people go home.
After the flowers fade, life keeps moving.
After the cards stop coming, the family still carries the baby.
A permanent place matters because grief does not end when the funeral ends.
Love does not end either.
For families who inherit cemetery plots, this is the invitation: do not see that space only as old paperwork or unused land.
See what it could become.
If your family no longer needs it, that plot may still have a purpose.
It may be the answer to a question another family is asking through tears.
It may become the place a mother or father visits because they have nowhere else to bring their love.
It may become the place where a baby’s name stays rooted in this world.
That is not a small thing.
That is legacy.
That is remembrance.
That is a gift that outlives the moment.
There are many ways to help grieving families. People can send meals. They can give money. They can sit quietly. They can say the baby’s name. They can remember birthdays and hard dates. All of that matters.
But a cemetery plot donation is different.
It creates a place.
A real place.
A place that can be visited.
A place that can hold a name.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
A baby may not have school pictures. They may not have birthday parties. They may not have years of stories everyone can remember. Sometimes there are only ultrasound pictures. Sometimes there are hospital photos. Sometimes there is a blanket, a bracelet, a tiny outfit, a memory box, a few sacred hours, or only the love a family carried before the world ever met them.
That does not make the life smaller.
It makes remembrance even more important.
**Protecting Memories Becomes Very Important**
Because when there are fewer visible memories, the ones that remain have to be protected.
I know this personally. When you lose a baby, you want people to understand that your child was not an idea. Not just a pregnancy. Not just a tragedy. Not just a painful chapter in your life.
Your child was your child.
Their name still means something.
Their place in the family is still real.
And if the world is going to move on, you still need somewhere that does not.
That is what a resting place can become.
Nobody wants to need it. No parent dreams of standing at their child’s grave. No family should ever have to think about burial while they are still trying to understand how they are breathing.
It is not natural.
It is not fair.
It is not how life is supposed to go.
But when it does happen, that place can become part of how a family survives.
You can go there when nobody knows what to say. You can sit there when you do not want advice. You can talk out loud. You can cry without explaining it. You can bring flowers, a toy, a letter, a drawing, a little stone, or nothing at all.
You can just be there.
And sometimes that is what love needs.
A place to be there.
**Giving Other Family Members and Friends a Way to Remember and Heal**
It also gives the rest of the family a way to remember. Children may not understand everything about death, but they understand bringing a flower. They understand drawing a picture. They understand visiting. They understand that this is where we go because this baby is part of us.
That matters.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
Because when a baby dies, there is often a quiet pressure to tuck the grief away. To not make people uncomfortable. To not bring it up too much. To not make every gathering sad. To not keep reminding people.
But a resting place says the opposite.
It says this child is not being tucked away.
This child is loved.
This child has a name.
This child has a place.
This child belongs.
**Your Burial Plot Donation Matters**
That is why donating a cemetery plot can be such a powerful act. It may look simple from the outside. It may look like unused land. It may look like something sitting there with no purpose anymore.
But to another family, it can become holy ground.
It can become the place where a baby’s name stays rooted in this world.
It can become the place a mother visits on the birthday nobody else remembers. The place a father stands when he has no words left. The place a family brings flowers because love still has nowhere else to go. The place where siblings learn that even the smallest life can leave a permanent mark.
**A Final Resting Place Goes Way Beyond Just a Donation**
That is not just a donation.
That is giving a child dignity.
That is giving a family somewhere to return.
That is giving love a place to keep showing up.
And for families who are already broken by loss, that gift can remove one more crushing burden. They are already trying to survive the impossible. They should not also have to wonder whether their baby can have a proper place. They should not have to make decisions from shock, fear, confusion, and financial pressure all at once.
No parent should have to fight for their child to be remembered.
No parent should have to feel like their baby’s place in the world depends on what they can afford during the worst days of their life.
A cemetery becomes more than a cemetery in this kind of grief.
It becomes the place where love continues in public.
Not loudly.
Not dramatically.
Quietly.
A name on a stone. A flower left behind. A small toy. A parent standing there longer than people would understand. A family returning year after year because the love did not end when the life did.
That is the part people need to understand.
Remembrance is not extra.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
It is not a nice add-on.
It is not just something sentimental people do because they cannot let go.
**Remembrance is How Love Refuses to Let a Child Disappear**
There are many baby memorial ideas that help families carry their child forward. Photos matter. Jewelry matters. Blankets matter. Memory boxes matter. Tattoos, ornaments, candles, gardens, letters, and songs can all become part of healing.
But a place is different.
A place stands outside of you.
A place tells the truth even when you are not there to explain it.
A place says to the world, “This child was here.”
That matters because baby loss is often invisible. People do not see the empty car seat that was never filled. They do not see the due date that still hurts. They do not see the birthday that comes every year. They do not see the parent doing the math in their head, wondering how old their child would be now.
They do not see the missing.
A place makes some of that missing visible.
Not to trap the family in grief.
But to honor the love that is still alive.
**Why We Care So Much About Remembrance**
That is why Pierced Forever cares so much about remembrance. Not because a grave can take away the pain. It cannot. Not because a plot or marker fixes what happened. It does not.
But because a child’s name deserves more than silence.
A child’s name deserves more than being remembered only in private tears.
A child’s name deserves a place in this world.
Some people reading this know this pain personally. Some love someone who knows it. Some may have something they could give that would become sacred to a family they may never meet.
And maybe that is the point.
Sometimes the most meaningful gift is not loud. It is not complicated. It is not seen by everyone.
Sometimes it is simply making room.
Room for a name.
Room for a family to grieve.
Room for love to return.
Room for a child’s place in this world to remain.
Because when a baby dies, the family does not stop being a family. The love does not stop being love. The name does not stop being a name.
And the child should not disappear just because the world does not know how to hold the grief.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
A child’s name matters.
A place matters.
A life matters, even if it was brief.
Every child deserves a place love can return to.
**Building a Lasting Memory for Your Child**
If you, or your family, have suffered the loss of a child turn to us for assistance in finding a burial plotthat will establish itself as the destination of remembrance and healing. Our team has personal experience in the loss of a child and is there for you when it feels like no one else is.## Brandon Movitz
I started writing because I know how lonely loss can feel, even when people care. Some things are easy to miss until life brings them close. Loss changes people. It changes families. It changes what help should look like.
My hope is that these words make the hard things clearer, the quiet needs easier to see, and the care people feel easier to turn into something that actually helps.

# Every grave holds a story. Sometimes, all it takes is a flower to remind us that someone is still remembered. 🌼 For this part of my October cemetery series, I’m sharing the grave of Mollie Herlihy Parlin at South Lead Cemetery in Lead, South Dakota. I visited her grave on her birthday, April 7th, at the request of a follower. He told me he had been bringing her a daisy every day, and since he couldn’t be there for her birthday, he asked if I would stop by. That simple act of kindness stayed with me. Online burial records list her as Mollie, born April 7, 1870, in Michigan. She passed away on April 10, 1892 ~ just three days after her 22nd birthday. FamilySearch also identifies her as the mother of a little boy, Franklin Kendrick Parlin, born less than two months before her death. As I looked around her grave, I didn’t notice any nearby headstones that appeared to belong to relatives. I don’t know her whole story, but there’s something about standing beside someone’s grave and taking a moment to wonder about the life behind the name. If you’re ever looking for a small, meaningful thing to do, stop by the grave of someone you don’t know. Bring flowers, pick up litter around their resting place, or simply spend a quiet moment thinking about their life. You don’t have to have known someone to remember them. 🙏 Stay tuned for more of my cemetery series throughout the month of October. ## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
​
But maybe if more people thought about them before another family had to, fewer parents would have to face that burden alone.
​There are cemetery plots sitting unused all over this country.
Most people do not think about them that way.
They think about them only when they are handling an estate, sorting through papers, cleaning out a parent’s house, or trying to figure out what to do with something that was purchased years ago by someone they loved. A deed. A burial right. A cemetery space. A plot in a place nobody in the family lives near anymore.
It might sit in a file cabinet.
It might be listed in estate paperwork.
It might come up after a mother or father passes away and the children are trying to divide responsibilities, close accounts, sell the house, finish the paperwork, and make decisions nobody really wants to make.
And buried inside all of that is a cemetery plot.
Maybe two.
Maybe more.
A space purchased decades ago that no longer fits the family plan. Maybe the person who bought it was buried somewhere else. Maybe the family moved. Maybe siblings now live in different states. Maybe cremation changed the original plan. Maybe nobody knows what to do with it, so it just sits there.
To that family, it may feel like one more loose end.
To another family, it could become sacred ground.
That is the part most people never see.
While thousands of cemetery plots sit unused, families who lose a child are often blindsided by the cost, confusion, and emotional weight of needing one.
Nobody prepares for that.
Young families are not thinking about cemetery plots. They are thinking about pregnancy, names, bottles, cribs, car seats, hospital bags, baby clothes, ultrasounds, birthdays, and the life they are trying to build.
They are not thinking about burial space.
They are not thinking about opening and closing fees.
They are not thinking about cemetery rules.
They are not thinking about where they would go if the unthinkable happened.
Then loss comes.
Planning after a loss
Sometimes during pregnancy. Sometimes at birth. Sometimes after days or weeks in the NICU. Sometimes suddenly, after a baby came home. Sometimes in a way no family ever saw coming.
And before the family can even understand what happened, the questions begin.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
*   Where will the baby be buried?

*   Is there a cemetery nearby?

*   Is there a section for infants?

*   How much does a burial plot cost?

*   What fees are separate?

*   \Can we afford this?

*   Who do we call?

*   What happens now?
Burial Plot FAQ
That is a terrible moment to learn how expensive and confusing burial can be.
And this is where people need to understand something deeper.
For a grieving family, this is not just “a funeral.”
A funeral is an event.
A burial place is different.
A funeral happens on a day. A permanent place to return to lasts for years. It becomes the place a parent visits when nobody knows what to say. The place where flowers are brought. The place where a sibling may bring a drawing. The place where a family can sit in silence because love still needs somewhere to go.
That place matters.
After infant loss, remembrance is not a small thing.
It is not extra.
It is not just sentimental.
It is one of the ways a family keeps their baby from disappearing into silence.
Because when a baby dies, the world often moves on quickly. People may stop saying the name. They may avoid bringing it up because they are afraid of causing pain. They may think silence is kindness.
But for the family, silence can feel like erasure.
A resting place helps push back against that.
It says, “This child was here.”
It says, “This life mattered.”
It says, “There is a place in this world connected to this name.”
That matters when the life was brief. It matters when there are not years of photos, stories, school pictures, birthday parties, and memories for the world to hold onto. It matters when the love was enormous, but the visible proof of that life feels painfully small.
A cemetery plot is not just land.
It is not just grass.
It is not just a square on a map.
For a baby, it can become the only public place in the world where their name stands permanently.
That is why unused cemetery plots matter so much.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
There are families right now holding onto burial spaces they may never use. Not because they are selfish. Not because they do not care. Most of the time, they probably have not even thought about what that space could mean to someone else.
It is just part of the estate.
Part of the paperwork.
Part of the past.
Something to deal with eventually.
But imagine looking at it differently.
Imagine that the plot your family no longer needs could become the place another family visits for the rest of their lives.
Imagine that instead of sitting unused, it becomes the place where a baby’s name remains in the world.
Imagine that a space connected to one family’s history could become mercy for another family’s heartbreak.
That is what cemetery plot donation can do.
It turns something forgotten into something holy.
It turns a loose end into a lasting gift.
It turns unused space into a place for love and memory.
And for the person donating, there may also be a practical benefit. A cemetery plot donation to a qualified nonprofit may be treated as a noncash charitable contribution, and donors should speak with their tax advisor about whether they may qualify for a tax deduction, what documentation is needed, and how the plot should be valued. The IRS says Form 8283 is generally used when claiming more than $500 in noncash charitable contributions, and deductions over $5,000 for noncash items generally require additional documentation such as Section B of Form 8283 and a qualified appraisal.
That matters.
Because sometimes people want to help but do not know how. Sometimes they are settling an estate and trying to make responsible decisions. Sometimes they are asking, “Can we sell this? Transfer it? Donate it? Is it worth anything? Does anyone need it?”
Yes.
Someone may need it more than you can imagine.
And while the tax benefit may help make the decision easier, the deeper value is not found on a form.
The deeper value is this:

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
*   A family who lost a baby may not have to fight for a place.

*   A child may have somewhere their name can remain.

*   Love may have somewhere to return.

*   I think about the families who visit years later.

*   Not only in the first week.

*   Not only on the day of burial.

*   Years later.
A parent standing there on a birthday that most people forgot. A family stopping by on a holiday. Someone bringing flowers on a day that still hurts. A sibling growing up and slowly understanding that there was another child in the family, a baby whose life was brief but whose place is still real.
People may not see those moments.
They happen quietly.
No big announcement.
No attention.
Just love returning to the same place again and again.
That is what a donated plot can make possible.
It gives a family more than help with child funeral costs. It gives them a place that continues after the funeral is over.
Because after the service ends, people go home.
After the flowers fade, life keeps moving.
After the cards stop coming, the family still carries the baby.
A permanent place matters because grief does not end when the funeral ends.
Love does not end either.
For families who inherit cemetery plots, this is the invitation: do not see that space only as old paperwork or unused land.
See what it could become.
If your family no longer needs it, that plot may still have a purpose.
It may be the answer to a question another family is asking through tears.
It may become the place a mother or father visits because they have nowhere else to bring their love.
It may become the place where a baby’s name stays rooted in this world.
That is not a small thing.
That is legacy.
That is remembrance.
That is a gift that outlives the moment.
There are many ways to help grieving families. People can send meals. They can give money. They can sit quietly. They can say the baby’s name. They can remember birthdays and hard dates. All of that matters.
But a cemetery plot donation is different.
It creates a place.
A real place.
A place that can be visited.
A place that can hold a name.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
A baby may not have school pictures. They may not have birthday parties. They may not have years of stories everyone can remember. Sometimes there are only ultrasound pictures. Sometimes there are hospital photos. Sometimes there is a blanket, a bracelet, a tiny outfit, a memory box, a few sacred hours, or only the love a family carried before the world ever met them.
That does not make the life smaller.
It makes remembrance even more important.
**Protecting Memories Becomes Very Important**
Because when there are fewer visible memories, the ones that remain have to be protected.
I know this personally. When you lose a baby, you want people to understand that your child was not an idea. Not just a pregnancy. Not just a tragedy. Not just a painful chapter in your life.
Your child was your child.
Their name still means something.
Their place in the family is still real.
And if the world is going to move on, you still need somewhere that does not.
That is what a resting place can become.
Nobody wants to need it. No parent dreams of standing at their child’s grave. No family should ever have to think about burial while they are still trying to understand how they are breathing.
It is not natural.
It is not fair.
It is not how life is supposed to go.
But when it does happen, that place can become part of how a family survives.
You can go there when nobody knows what to say. You can sit there when you do not want advice. You can talk out loud. You can cry without explaining it. You can bring flowers, a toy, a letter, a drawing, a little stone, or nothing at all.
You can just be there.
And sometimes that is what love needs.
A place to be there.
**Giving Other Family Members and Friends a Way to Remember and Heal**
It also gives the rest of the family a way to remember. Children may not understand everything about death, but they understand bringing a flower. They understand drawing a picture. They understand visiting. They understand that this is where we go because this baby is part of us.
That matters.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
Because when a baby dies, there is often a quiet pressure to tuck the grief away. To not make people uncomfortable. To not bring it up too much. To not make every gathering sad. To not keep reminding people.
But a resting place says the opposite.
It says this child is not being tucked away.
This child is loved.
This child has a name.
This child has a place.
This child belongs.
**Your Burial Plot Donation Matters**
That is why donating a cemetery plot can be such a powerful act. It may look simple from the outside. It may look like unused land. It may look like something sitting there with no purpose anymore.
But to another family, it can become holy ground.
It can become the place where a baby’s name stays rooted in this world.
It can become the place a mother visits on the birthday nobody else remembers. The place a father stands when he has no words left. The place a family brings flowers because love still has nowhere else to go. The place where siblings learn that even the smallest life can leave a permanent mark.
**A Final Resting Place Goes Way Beyond Just a Donation**
That is not just a donation.
That is giving a child dignity.
That is giving a family somewhere to return.
That is giving love a place to keep showing up.
And for families who are already broken by loss, that gift can remove one more crushing burden. They are already trying to survive the impossible. They should not also have to wonder whether their baby can have a proper place. They should not have to make decisions from shock, fear, confusion, and financial pressure all at once.
No parent should have to fight for their child to be remembered.
No parent should have to feel like their baby’s place in the world depends on what they can afford during the worst days of their life.
A cemetery becomes more than a cemetery in this kind of grief.
It becomes the place where love continues in public.
Not loudly.
Not dramatically.
Quietly.
A name on a stone. A flower left behind. A small toy. A parent standing there longer than people would understand. A family returning year after year because the love did not end when the life did.
That is the part people need to understand.
Remembrance is not extra.

## People worry so much about saying the wrong thing that sometimes they say nothing.
It is not a nice add-on.
It is not just something sentimental people do because they cannot let go.
**Remembrance is How Love Refuses to Let a Child Disappear**
There are many baby memorial ideas that help families carry their child forward. Photos matter. Jewelry matters. Blankets matter. Memory boxes matter. Tattoos, ornaments, candles, gardens, letters, and songs can all become part of healing.
But a place is different.
A place stands outside of you.
A place tells the truth even when you are not there to explain it.
A place says to the world, “This child was here.”
That matters because baby loss is often invisible. People do not see the empty car seat that was never filled. They do not see the due date that still hurts. They do not see the birthday that comes every year. They do not see the parent doing the math in their head, wondering how old their child would be now.
They do not see the missing.
A place makes some of that missing visible.
Not to trap the family in grief.
But to honor the love that is still alive.
**Why We Care So Much About Remembrance**
That is why Pierced Forever cares so much about remembrance. Not because a grave can take away the pain. It cannot. Not because a plot or marker fixes what happened. It does not.
But because a child’s name deserves more than silence.
A child’s name deserves more than being remembered only in private tears.
A child’s name deserves a place in this world.
Some people reading this know this pain personally. Some love someone who knows it. Some may have something they could give that would become sacred to a family they may never meet.
And maybe that is the point.
Sometimes the most meaningful gift is not loud. It is not complicated. It is not seen by everyone.
Sometimes it is simply making room.
Room for a name.
Room for a family to grieve.
Room for love to return.
Room for a child’s place in this world to remain.
Because when a baby dies, the family does not stop being a family. The love does not stop being love. The name does not stop being a name.
And the child should not disappear just because the world does not know how to hold the grief.
